https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07: British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.
It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' ( Natsal , external ) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.
Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.
But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.
Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.
More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year.
Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it.

Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure.
They didn't ask about AI or virtual relationships with romantic chatbots, but say they probably should next time.
Soazig Clifton, one of the Natsal team and from University College London, said: "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi.
"In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behaviour and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."

Co-researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), says while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, "especially for young people."
Young people are drinking less alcohol than past generations and more live at home with their parents, for example.
Rising rates of mental health conditions might also be involved, along with the Covid pandemic that stopped people going out.
She says more open discussion of consent could also mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex.
One in seven women (14%) reported ongoing upset with others about things done to them in their sexual past.
The same proportion of men reported feeling shame about some of their sexual thoughts and desires.
This fourth Natsal survey reveals trends, but cannot fully explain them.
The previous one, in 2010, suggested having sex too soon was the biggest regret of young people losing their virginity.
Almost two in five young women (38%) and more than one in four young men (28%) now report never having had sex. That is up from around one in five in the earlier surveys of 1990, 2000 and 2010.
And among all adults who are having sex, most are doing it less often. The average used to be once a week. Now, it's fortnightly.
The latest results, published in The Lancet and based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16-59 selected at random across Britain, reveal:
women have sex once a month and men twice a month, on average
reports of sex with a same-sex partner have increased among both men and women, but by how much is less clear
Many Brits, young people in particular, are having unprotected sex that can lead to pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), the figures suggest.
And use of the oral contraceptive pill has declined among young women.
But more women now say they do not want children - a doubling in the past decade, from 8% to 17% among those aged 16–44.

"Understanding what's driving this – whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety or changing life priorities – should now be a priority for future research and policy, as it has real implications for planning health, care and family services," says researcher Dr Laura Oakley from the LSHTM.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm: Ayana Bailey says she relies on her mum to go through the job application process with her
Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.
"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.
A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.
Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.
Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.
For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.
In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."
One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.
Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.
"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."
She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.
For nurse Lisa Daniels, her dyslexia meant leaving work more than an hour late most days just to finish the paperwork.
"I suppressed it. I was like 'Oh no, everything is fine. It's not affecting me.'" In reality, she says "it was majorly affecting me".
Daniels, 37, says a previous manager was dismissive of her request for adjustments.
"When I first started, they said, 'Oh they are babying some of these nurses' and I didn't have the confidence to challenge it."
She says her suggestions of having more accessible fonts and colours on documents were not listened to.
Five years into her career, Daniels' colleague told her about a staff network on neurodiversity and her confidence grew, along with adjustments such as noise-cancelling headphones.
"I have that resilience that, despite the sometimes lack of support, I'm still gonna show up. I'm still gonna try."
Lisa Daniels says she has built up her resilience despite previous bad experiences at work
Over half of people surveyed by the BDA say dyslexia makes them feel bad about themselves, while 39% have experienced bad mental health related to it.
The BDA is calling for workplaces to make reasonable adjustments for employees who need them, even without a diagnosis, and wants managers to be trained to understand and support dyslexic employees.
Its report finds dyslexic employees often have to put extra effort into work, finding their own ways to cope if systems, processes and communication are not accessible.
There are 3.3 million dyslexic adults currently in employment, estimates the BDA. Some told the report:
"I have to cope with little comments that are seen as banter about my spelling."
"My line manager is actually dyslexic and we happily talk about it. We share best practice and war stories."
"It would be nice to be seen as intellectual. Just because I cannot always write as well as others, doesn't mean I don't have the knowledge."
"I revealed my dyslexia quite early on in my employment… I do believe it was used as a stick to beat me with."
"I feel like I have got to do more, be more, show more... because I've got this deficit of being dyslexic".
Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client win a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case against Starbucks in 2016.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpd: Prof Fiona Gilbert, who is co-leading the trial, will assess if AI can improve breast cancer diagnosis
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.
AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.
Recruitment to the EDITH trial , external has already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.
Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.
At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."
Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.
About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.
It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.

"Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment."
Gilbert told the BBC there was a "huge shortfall" in radiologists and that the number of imaging examinations was increasing by 8% a year.
Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.
She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.
She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms."
Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.
"I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.
Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.
The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.
Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.

Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.
In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts. In another, it will review images afterwards.
The £10m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).
It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98: Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.
Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."
Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.
Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.
The sleeping bag is now unavailable on Next's website after safety fears were raised

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."
Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

In an article on the British Retail Consortium (BRC) website, safety science company UL Solutions explains that a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.
They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."
To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.
For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.
Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.
After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.
"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"
Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.
Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.
She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.
"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.
"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"
Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.
But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.
Emma's baby Rosie is now 3 and a half months old and uses a different sleeping bag
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible. Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatment

Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.
Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.
just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.
Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.
Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."
He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC–NCI–AACR Symposium 2026 , external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."
Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year , external .
In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: More than 200 doctors have had their details sent in error to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw: Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but must be rooted in evidence, the regulator said
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.
It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.
Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.
The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.
Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.
Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".
At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.
Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations
The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".
The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.
It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".
The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.
The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.
This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.
The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0e: From Spring 2027, under 16s will no longer be able to access several social media applications
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.
The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.
Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.
The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Apps such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat and YouTube will be banned under new rules
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

There have also been reports of Australian teens finding ways to get round the ban - with the UK government promising to make sure tougher blocks are in place.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9zr: Carol Shillabeer joined as chief executive of Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board in May 2023
The chief executive of Wales's largest health board will no longer take up a new post in England, following a damning review of her current organisation's leadership.
Carol Shillabeer, who has been Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board's chief executive since May 2023, had been due to lead the Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Trust in England in the new year.
But a review into the Welsh health board found that, in some parts, targets and money had a "greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".
The Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said the "seriousness of the findings" could not be ignored and Shillabeer made the "personal decision" to withdraw from the role.
Dyfed Edwards, chair of Betsi Cadwaladr health board, confirmed Shillabeer would leave her current post on 3 January 2027. He thanked her for her service and wished her well for the future.
Confirming Shillabeer's withdrawal from the role, the Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said it had "taken our time to carefully consider the situation and discuss the matter" with her.
"Carol feels that this is the best course of action for the sake of the patients, our communities, and LSCFT staff."
"We agree with her decision and wish her the best for the future," it added.
A spokesperson said that a board of trustees would consider the next steps regarding the appointment of a new chief executive.

Shillabeer spent three and a half years leading the health board, which covers all of north Wales. She was appointed after the Welsh government put it into "special measures" for the second time in its history.
It has been under the highest level of oversight due to concerns about care quality, patient safety and leadership .
Betsi Cadwaladr health board has been beset by problems since its inception in 2009
The independent review published on Tuesday found the health board lacked "the organisational conditions necessary to reliably deliver and sustain improvement".
It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.
It also said the health board had a "dedicated and loyal" workforce, with a "high level of expertise" across many services, as well as the capacity to provide strong local services.
The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".
Responding to the document, Health Minister, Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, rejected calls for "radical action or structural change".
Instead, he suggested that "stability" is needed following a period characterised by "too much change."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg: Shauna said the future had been "ripped apart" after her partner, Row, was diagnosed with very severe ME
Rowena Davies had been planning to travel the world with her partner until an ME diagnosis left her unable to talk or leave her bed.

The 42-year-old, known as Row, initially thought she was burnt out, but after years of searching for answers was finally diagnosed in 2021 and her partner Shauna Chambers has since given up work to help the family care for her.
Campaigners are warning that people with severe ME - sometimes referred to clinically as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome - could die without changes to services in Wales.
The Welsh government said proposals for an all‑Wales specialist, an expert group and national standards were being considered.
It is estimated more than 400,000 people across the UK have ME, a complex multi-system condition with no known cure.
Shauna, 34, said: "She had a cough that didn't leave for many months, but the main thing was that she would be absolutely drained and exhausted after doing such small things.
Row loves being outdoors but she's now been in bed for five years
Shauna, from Tywyn in Gwynedd, said Row was "full of energy" and loved sport, but now she cannot tolerate light or noise, and any exertion will cause her to deteriorate.
"We feed her, we wash her, we brush her teeth. We were left to navigate this on our own," she said.
"It's like you're grieving someone that is still alive, and you sit next to her sometimes, and all you can do is just hold her hand and breathe.
"People's lives have been completely ruined by this condition, and if nothing changes people can die from ME, and it is absolutely avoidable."
Campaigners told BBC Wales in March that healthcare services were "like a desert" for those most severely affected.
Shauna has been campaigning on behalf of her partner and other patients in Wales

With the right support, Row's family are hopeful she can get better. She recently had her first visit by the Living Well service within Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which has been expanded to include ME, and now aims to support people living with any severity of the condition.
It uses funding from the Welsh government's Adferiad programme , external but campaigners say that services vary between health boards. There is no clinical lead for ME in Wales.
John Peters, 65, from Swansea, was diagnosed with the condition 40 years ago. He was once a keen rugby player, but after a virus, his life changed.
"I've gone through improvements, and then got another infection, and that's been the cycle of my life since 1985," he said.
"One of the hardest things is the loss of identity. You're not a husband, a father, you don't have a career.
"Your life goes past and then you realise what's happened. I hate the illness.
"No one knows what I've been through. There is no care for me."

Swansea Bay University Health Board said its service, also funded by the Adferiad programme, "focuses on improving quality of life, supporting independence, and enabling individuals to manage the impact of ME within their own daily circumstances" while "recognising the fluctuating nature of the condition and the importance of personalised care".
ME is a chronic and complex multi-system condition, which causes symptoms such as extreme fatigue and post-exertional malaise.
That means simple physical or mental activities can leave people completely debilitated.
Not everyone with ME is affected in the same way. There is a spectrum of severity, which is often categorised as mild, moderate, severe and very severe.
While researchers are still investigating the causes, triggers may include infection or other illness. There is no specific treatment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwe9: Volunteers from local communities have been involved in setting out the plants
Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.
The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.
The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.
Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.
Ellen Hebdon says the plants' roots play an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water
The islands are manufactured by a Moray-based company which has been exporting them around the world.
Biomatrix Water Solutions in Forres has installed islands in Boston, Venice and London.
They have also been floated onto the River Clyde at the Glasgow Science Centre as part of an unrelated project.
The new islands are being installed at Victoria Park, Elder Park, Richmond Park, Queen's Park and Hogganfield Loch.
Ellen Hebdon, the company's operations manager, said the plants' roots played an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water.
"It's not an overnight solution, but over a period of time, you will see benefits in the clarity and the cleanliness of the water," she said.
Floating islands have been installed at the Glasgow Science Centre
The islands are made up of recycled plastic materials, including drinking water pipes, to create buoyancy and are held together using marine-grade stainless steel.
They are then topped with a lightweight clay aggregate, called leca, into which the plants are inserted.
The aquatic plants include a mix of evergreen and flowering native species such as marsh marigolds, water forget-me-nots and ragged robin.
Their roots underneath the islands provide shelter for aquatic wildlife.
The location, in the middle of the water, also provides nesting spaces for birds, which would be largely free from disturbance.
Local schools and "friends of the park" groups are helping with the planting and maintenance.

Games organisers say sustainability is an important delivery factor with all competition venues powered by renewable electricity and electric or hybrid vehicles making up two thirds of the transport fleet.
Glasgow 2026's head of sustainability, Selina Donald, said the city council had been looking at creating floating islands but did not have the funding.

"I really saw the pride in all the parks, the pride in the green spaces, the pride in the natural environment across the city," she said. "And so really, for us, it was a way that we can celebrate and support that."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckm2: Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.
Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.
FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4: Campaigners worried the mining could impact sea turtles in the area

The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.
Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.
The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.
The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.
The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.
Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.

Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.

Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment. , external However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.
In one study of the impact of deep-sea mining, researchers found more than 4,000 animals, 90% of which were new species, living on the seafloor in a remote area of the Pacific Ocean.
Some critics of the industry fear that before we have the chance to explore the full nature of life in the undiscovered deep ocean, it could be endangered.
The leatherback sea turtle is listed as endangered under the ESA
Norway was the first country in the world to approve commercial-scale deep-sea mining in 2024 .
Over 2,000 of the world's scientists met in 2025 to review the data on ocean health and they recommended governments halt deep sea exploration while further research on the impacts was carried out.
More than 30 countries supported this position and called for a moratorium.
Shortly before that meeting, President Trump published executive orders to push ahead with mining and "unleash America's offshore critical minerals and resources".
He said "these resources are key to strengthening our economy, securing our energy future, and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers for critical minerals".
Part of the plan aims to "counter China's growing influence over seabed mineral resources".
Deep-sea mining targets polymetallic nodules , external – potato-sized rocks found over 4,000 metres below the ocean surface.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg7: Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site

The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the controlled detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa: an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday following the detonation around the ammunition plant, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
An all-clear was issued. Local soil, air and water continue to be tested.
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.
In an update late on Wednesday, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead after the controlled explosion.

He wrote on X that the agency would "continue to be radically transparent with the public as sample results come in from the laboratory", and that these were "projected to start arriving back over the next 24 to 48 hours".
His post added: "Our goal is to complete ALL sampling by tomorrow and will remain on the ground to complete any remediation if at all necessary."

More than 1,000 post-detonation samples had been taken from homes, parks, farms and drinking water taps among other locations, Zeldin said. On Thursday, sites including churches, schools and playgrounds would be sampled as well.
President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation. This made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.
Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the all-clear around the plant, adding: "Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete."
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Sandy Mabeus was also eight miles from Middletown. She closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."

Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.
"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8: Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.
Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.
In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.
The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.
"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.
"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.
"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."
The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.
Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.
On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.
Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.
Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.
Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.
In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.
The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.
Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.
The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record , according to provisional Met Office data.
There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.
Tim Young's onions have been smaller than usual making them harder to sell to supermarkets

"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.
This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.
Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.
"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.
Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.
Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.
It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".
Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.
But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: The asteroid before (left) and after, showing the crater left behind by a spacecraft's impact
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
Watch: Moment Nasa spacecraft leaves stadium-sized crater in asteroid
A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.
Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves.
"Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan.

"Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."
Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail.
"The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team.
"We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders.

"The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."
The mission has sent back new pictures of the smaller Dimorphos orbiting around Didymos
The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0: Fines will rise steeply for both littering and more serious fly-tipping offences
People caught littering or illegally dumping waste in a north-west London borough are set to face higher fines as the council steps up its efforts to tackle persistent fly-tipping.
Harrow Council has approved plans to increase penalties for littering, breaches of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) and the most serious fly-tipping offences.
Penalties for littering will rise from £500 to £750, with a reduced penalty of £300 available for early payment - the highest to be introduced in the capital under a new national maximum cap.
The penalty for breaching a PSPO will increase from £100 to £500, while a new £5,000 penalty will be introduced for the most serious fly-tipping offences.
The changes follow an increase in the maximum penalties available to councils under government rules.
The highest fly-tipping penalty will only be used in cases involving "aggravating factors", such as hazardous waste or repeat offences.
Other factors include the dumping of multiple bags, whether the waste affects vulnerable people, and whether it was dumped by a business for financial gain.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting where the proposal was approved last week, councillor Pritesh Patel said: "The reason for these changes is that the government has increased the maximum penalties available to councils. This gives us an opportunity to strengthen our response to environmental crime.
"Most people do the right thing, but there is a minority that don't, and it is important that the consequences are meaningful and encourage prompt compliance and resolutions."
Harrow Council has previously been criticised for its handling of fly-tipping

Harrow Council has tried a number of approaches to tackle fly-tipping over the years, including installing CCTV cameras in hotspots, sharing images and videos of offenders on social media and taking people to court.
But in January 2026, the council was criticised for failing to prosecute enough offenders at a fly-tipping hotspot in Harrow Weald.
Residents said a site on Weighton Road had to be cleared every few days. Despite a CCTV camera being in operation, only seven people had been sanctioned in the previous year.
One resident told a cabinet meeting in February that seven fines could be issued in a week, "let alone 52".
At the time, the council described the situation as "disgusting" following the long-running problems.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/2: Invasive freshwater clams have been detected at Atiamuri Hydro Station on the Waikato River, outside the existing controlled area.
Biosecurity New Zealand has confirmed the presence of Corbicula clams, likely C. fluminea , commonly known as 'gold clams', at the hydro station.
It is the first confirmed detection outside the controlled area upstream from Whakamaru Dam.
National Corbicula Programme Manager Lisa Hargegger said the discovery highlighted how easily the clams can spread.
"Juvenile clams can be smaller than a grain of sand. You don't necessarily have to see one to spread one."
Waikato Regional Council, Biosecurity New Zealand, Waikato River iwi and other partners are working to establish the extent of the spread.
Surveillance of high-risk waterways is also continuing this summer.

Waikato Regional Council integrated catchment management director Greg Ryan said the discovery was a reminder that there was no room for complacency when it came to protecting Aotearoa's lakes and rivers.

"We've all invested significant time and effort into slowing the spread of freshwater clams. Now more than ever, we need people to keep doing the small things that make a difference, including checking, cleaning and drying equipment before leaving the water," he said.
Waikato Regional Council said ballast tanks in boats were considered a particular risk because they could hold water containing microscopic juvenile clams.
Although there were currently no specific restrictions on ballasted boats in this part of the river, owners were being encouraged to avoid moving their vessels between waterways where possible.
Freshwater clams reproduce rapidly and can establish large populations in a short time.
Once established, they are extremely difficult to control and can threaten native species, water infrastructure and the economy.
It is illegal to knowingly move the clams or water containing them.
People should not collect or eat the clams, as they can accumulate harmful contaminants.

Anyone who suspects they have found the clams outside the Waikato River should take a photo, note the location and report it to Biosecurity New Zealand on 0800 809 966 or through its online reporting form.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/science-and-t: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/science-and-technology/2827264%2Felon-musk-s-1-million-starmind-satellites-a-land-grab-auckland-professor-says
An Auckland professor says US trillionaire Elon Musk's move to put one million satellites into space - newly dubbed 'Starmind' - is like a "land grab".
Another researcher said the data centre satellites with solar arrays would be so big and bright they'd change the night sky from the likes of Mount John Observatory near Tekapo forever.
Elon Musk has already launched over 11,000 satellites mostly for his Internet provider Starlink - far more than the US and Chinese governments combined.
Now the Trump administration has given his company SpaceX the okay to deploy a million more to run data centres on 24-hour sunlight.
Richard Easther from Auckland University's department of physics said it is at the limits of what's feasible to harvest energy and cool the computing.

"The best way to get heat out of something is to have something cold touch it. And so space is cold but the only way to get rid of heat is what we call radiation ... that's the only option you've got for getting rid of heat in space," said Easther on Friday.
The US Federal Communications Commission has approved the plan , calling it an ingenious step into a bold frontier for America's "booming super-intelligence economy".
"Super intelligence" was repurposed by Donald Trump as the White House's name for artificial intelligence recently.
"If you can launch a lot of satellites very quickly, then that kind of gives you at least an informal right to have that amount of material in space.
"[It's] very much an attempt to exploit the fact that there are no clear norms about this kind of behaviour ... like, you know, a rush to claim land on a gold field."
Unlike a neighbourhood in Auckland, say, there were no planning rules in space, Easther said.
Musk has his own rockets so no new launch business may come anyone else's way.
While one worry is that other countries' digital sovereignty may flow to him.
Lecturer in AI Dr Kerry McInerney said for both business and politics, this is a bad idea.
"There's a really strong argument against one person and one company having such outsized power over our digital infrastructure," she said on Friday.
"Right now Elon Musk's companies already operate the vast majority of satellites in space and this would continue to further expand the amount of control that they have.

"And this has real implications because right now we're already moving towards a world where two countries, the US and China, provide the world with so much of the digital infrastructure we use on a daily basis. And so that puts countries like Aotearoa in a tricky situation."
Already Starlink satellites fall out of the sky at a regular rate as they only last a few years.
But they are much much smaller than a data centre satellite that would also require terrific energy and fuel to launch.
All those processes, fuelling and falling en masse, are a prospect that is disturbing environmental researchers.
Professor Laura Revell of Canterbury University said a million satellites would be arguably the "largest experiment in atmospheric chemistry" the world has ever seen.
"That would mean launching about eight satellites per hour from now until their deadline to complete the authorised constellation of 25 November, 2040," she told the Science Media Centre.
"We already know that emissions from rocket launches can cause depletion of the protective ozone layer."
Depletion has so far been insignificant due to low launch rates, she said - but maybe not for long.

Maintaining the "status quo" on New Zealand's climate commitments would largely fulfil one of Opportunity's bottom lines, party leader Qiulae Wong says.
The final election count, released today, erased the incumbent coalition's majority and leaves Christopher Luxon reliant on Opportunity's support to break the deadlock.

Opportunity laid out five bottom lines for coalition negotiations ahead of the election, including one to recommit to New Zealand's Paris Agreement obligations and protect the Climate Change Commission's independence.
Following today's results, Wong was asked to clarify what that meant.
"Our bottom line on climate change is largely about preserving the status quo and we have to do that, because that is under threat at the moment," she said.
"We've got parties that are threatening to remove the Climate Change Commission and to withdraw from Paris altogether."
There was "a lot more" that the party would like to do on climate change beyond that, "but that is our minimum bottom line", she said.
Each of Opportunity's potential coalition partners on the right went into the election with a different stance on that bottom line.
Christopher Luxon said staying in the Paris Agreement was also a non-negotiable for National in coalition negotiations.
National Party leader Christopher Luxon applauds supporters at the National Party 2026 election night event at the Viaduct Events Centre.

"It's in New Zealand's interest to be in the Paris Agreement, because as soon as we would come out, we're in bad company, there's only four countries that have pulled out," he told Morning Report in August.
Doing so would make the country poorer, because New Zealand products would be "kicked off the shelves" overseas, Luxon said.

New Zealand has pledged to halve its emissions by 2030, as its first nationally determined contribution to the Paris Agreement goal of maintaining global temperatures below 2°C of warming, and 'pursue efforts' to limit warming to 1.5°C.

However, current trajectories show that New Zealand will miss its pledge by a full year of emissions, and Luxon and other incumbent ministers have previously ruled out paying billions of dollars for overseas carbon credits to make up the shortfall.
Opportunity has said that it supports meeting the NDC and the only realistic way to do so now is through purchasing offshore credits.
National also supports retaining the Climate Change Commission, though the government removed some of its consultation and advice requirements in the last term.
New Zealand First strongly opposes remaining in the Paris Agreement.
It wants the country to withdraw from it altogether, arguing meeting the target could cost the country up to $22 billion in offshore credits.
The party does not have a specific policy on the Climate Change Commission, although deputy leader Shane Jones, in particular, has been critical of its advice.

ACT, on the other hand, wants to abolish the commission, transferring its responsibility for assessing progress towards emissions targets to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport.
It also proposes repealing the Zero Carbon Act , and the 2050 net-zero target for long-lived gases that is enshrined in that law.

The final election count has confirmed the results across Aotearoa's Māori electorates, with Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards extending his winning margin in Te Tai Tokerau to 583 votes.
The result means Te Pāti Māori will bring five MPs into Parliament, with four overhang seats.
It also denies Green MP Hūhana Lyndon a historic first win for the Greens in the Māori seats.
Edwards led by 436 votes ahead of Lyndon, Labour's Willow-Jean Prime and incumbent Mariameno Kapa-Kingi.
In a statement posted online Aperahama Edwards said he was honoured to have been elected to represent Te Tai Tokerau.
He thanked the voters, his campaign team and the volunteers who supported him.
He acknowledged the other candidates, saying they are "connected by whakapapa and a shared commitment to serve our people and our rohe."
"I enter Parliament knowing where I come from and who I am there to serve. Te Tai Tokerau is the kaitiaki of He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
"Our tūpuna left us with a responsibility to stand for the mana of our people, our whenua and our mokopuna. I will carry that responsibility with me."

Green Party candidate Hūhana Lyndon told RNZ she was grateful for the thousands of votes she received, and said the Greens' increased support across the Māori electorates was something the party did not take for granted.
She said her campaign, alongside her mahi in Parliament, in communities and on marae, had helped demonstrate there was support for the Greens in the electorate.
"Those over 9,000, nearly 10,000 votes that tautoko me demonstrate that there is tautoko for a green voice in Tai Tokerau," she said.
The party vote in Te Tai Tokerau gave 36.9 percent of votes to the Green Party.
"So it's an absolute privilege to have that level of tautoko, and is something we do not take for granted."
Lyndon will remain in Parliament as a Green list MP, but said her next steps would need to be considered carefully.

She said campaigning on the basis of being an electorate MP meant she had planned to have offices open and kaimahi visible on the ground in Te Tai Tokerau. Being a list MP changed that, she said, and she had previously acknowledged her workload was not sustainable.
"We're going to go on to wānanga next week as the Greens. We will see what happens in terms of where we go on the forming of government. That will inform a lot," she said.

"But whether we're in government or in opposition as the Greens, we will be staunch in the way that we represent te taiao and protecting te taiao and also looking out for the wellbeing of our people and our places."

The official election results have left Parliament evenly split, with National, ACT and New Zealand First holding 65 seats, the same number as Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity combined.
