Auckland Council has approved plans for a Ferris wheel to open on the downtown waterfront this summer, close to where cruise ships moor.
There's no opening date yet but the 32-metre-tall attraction will have 24 gondolas holding up to 144 people on the Quay Street promenade.
Nighttime light displays will illuminate the Ferris wheel with audio telling the story of Tāmaki Makaurau.
Auckland mayor Wayne Brown said it is part of our bigger plan to open up more of the waterfront to the public.
"It's about making the most of one of our greatest assets; our stunning harbours," he said.

"The Ferris Wheel is part of a trial that will help us understand how people use this space and inform future waterfront planning and activation through the Central Wharves Masterplan and Long-term Plan, which the public will be consulted on."
Once up and running, the ferris wheel will be open from 10am till 10pm, extended till 11pm on public and school holidays and 12.30am on New Years Eve.
Skyline Attractions will operate the wheel on the Queens Wharf Breastworks, the waterfront promenade near the Downtown Ferry Terminal.
The proposal drew concern from local residents, concerned about their views and also what Ferris wheel riders might see from their goldolas.
The Auckland City Centre Residents' Group held a meeting to discuss their concerns about the plans earlier this month.

Maryanne and Alan Mummery have lived in an apartment building on Quay Street for more than 33 years and earlier said the wheel would be metres from their bedroom, and would affect the entire apartment building, as well as others around them.

"What a 30-plus years it has been. We've watched a complete reshaping of our waterfront and our much-loved port. The Hilton Hotel was built, The Cloud was built, all the wharf sheds, apart from Shed 10, were pulled down. Covid arrived. And now, in 2026, the most bizarre suggestion of all: a giant Ferris wheel right opposite the living spaces of hundreds of people," Maryanne Mummery said.
"Not only did we not know about this outrageous absurdity, it simply is an untenable suggestion for a small piece of port-gifted recreational land."
She said that the Council had been encouraging people to move into the CBD, but the wheel would end any sense of privacy for them and their neighbours.
"You can't sit in your bed with hundreds of people, sitting, gawping at you."
Auckland Council's Manager Premium Unit, Planning and Resource Consents, Dean Wiliams, granted the resource consent.

"Although a relatively large structure, the Ferris wheel is also a predominantly open, lattice type structure allowing views through it such that will not be physically dominant in form," he said in the report.
"The applicant has positioned the structure so that it sits at the end of Commerce Street rather than directly in front of neighbouring buildings on the opposite side of Quay Street."
Williams said that adverse effects on the landscape will be minimised and the outlook to the north for neighbours will still largely be preserved.
"The placement of the Ferris wheel, coupled with the separation distance and elements of the operation will ensure that any privacy effects are minimised."

"In terms of positive effects, the proposal utilises vacant land and provides a high-quality temporary visitor attraction. The project will contribute to the city centres vibrancy and amenity, providing social, economic, environmental, and cultural benefits," he said.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/crime-and-jus: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/crime-and-justice/2806979%2Fkaikohe-killing-man-who-fatally-stabbed-estene-rapatini-found-not-criminally-responsible
Warnings were raised, help was sought and police were alerted, but nothing stopped a mentally unwell man from killing Estene Rapatini.
Consumed by delusions, he believed he was protecting others from "eternal damnation" when he carried out the killing.

This week, the man, whose name is suppressed, appeared via audio-visual link from the Mason Clinic in the High Court at Whangārei, where Justice Amokura Kawharu ruled he was not criminally responsible on account of insanity.
Rapatini's death occurred on the same day as another killing in Whangārei, committed by a man who was also later found to be insane at the time of the offending.
On March 15, 2025, the man stabbed Rapatini, of Kaikohe, and his dog, killing them both.
He was charged with murder and the case then experienced several delays as determinations were made about his state of mind at the time of offending.
At the recent hearing, the 40-year-old was found to have a documented 30-year history of mental health issues, including schizophrenia.

Dr Himadri Seth told the court that in the days and months before the homicide, the man had delusional thinking, hallucinations and what the psychiatrist described as "a disease of the mind". This is one of the requirements for being determined unfit to stand trial which he said could often change.
He claimed he was acting to protect another person when he killed the victim.
He also believed the victim and gang members were conspiring to kill him and that he started co-ordinating a "hui telepathically".
"Obviously it didn't work and no one turned up," Dr Seth said.
By this point, Dr Seth said the man was acute. He was hearing dogs barking, gunshots, seeing footprints outside, experiencing psychological harassment and severe sleep deprivation.
He said the man believed he had no option but to kill Rapatini to protect others from the "eternal damnation" he feared.
"It was so severe there was no alternative. Morally, he felt he couldn't do anything else to end the thoughts and suffering in his mind."
Dr Seth said when the man was asked why he had not called police, he replied they could not help him.
"When someone is psychotic, there is no alternative," Dr Seth said.
Justice Kawharu noted that even people who are not legally insane sometimes hold similar views about police.
The man had also not complied with his mental health community order and had contacted mental health services the day before killing Rapatini.
Dr Seth said the man was not on the correct medication and had become treatment-resistant.
A week before the killing, a family member had called Kaikohe police and reported the man was "unhinged".
"The officer who took that phone call did not go to the property and investigate further.
"There were strong signs leading up to this and unfortunately it wasn't addressed."
Since the man has been in custody, psychologists said he was at times aggressive and unable to explain his options for entering a plea.
Although his symptoms had improved, psychologists said he continued to show signs of hallucinations and impaired engagement.
Justice Kawharu declared the man not unfit to stand trial but that he was insane at the time of the offending.
"You are not criminally responsible for these acts on account of insanity. You will be acquitted but that does not mean you will go free."
A further hearing will take place to determine final treatment orders, which could include continued detention at a secure mental health facility.

Rural Communities Minister Mark Patterson says the RNZ proposal to cut some of its rural news team is "extremely disappointing".
The proposed cuts to the rural team emerged on Thursday at the public broadcaster, along with plans to reduce the RNZ Asia, technology, and business news teams.
The cuts were in response to RNZ's financial problems, and amid the revelation of a $12 million deficit.
In a statement Friday, Patterson said he was "particularly concerned about the impact this proposal would have on what many are already describing as a growing 'news desert' across New Zealand".
He said rural reporting "ensures that the perspectives, challenges and successes of rural communities are visible and understood by the wider public".

"Rural New Zealand should not be paying the price for RNZ's financial mismanagement. If RNZ needs to find savings after a period of excessive overspending, it should start by examining its layers of management and bureaucracy, not by cutting frontline rural journalists," the NZ First MP said.

"Quality rural journalism is not a luxury, it is a public good. It supports informed decision-making, strengthens democratic participation, and ensures rural New Zealand has a voice in national conversations.

"I strongly encourage RNZ to reconsider this proposal and explore alternatives that preserve frontline rural reporting capacity. New Zealand needs more coverage of the industries and communities that underpin our economy, not less.

"As Minister for Rural Communities, I will continue to advocate for the importance of strong rural media coverage and for ensuring the voices of rural New Zealand continue to be heard," Patterson said.
Patterson said the incoming Media and Communications Minister needed to put the proposal at the "absolute top or their priority list".

"We can't have cuts to these critical rural services, it's not Radio Auckland or Radio Wellington, it's Radio New Zealand and it needs to be able to meet its charter and the minister and the incoming government need to make sure that continues to happen."
He said RNZ needed to "cut its cloth" in response to its financial situation.

"But the wrong people are paying the price, not only ... the valued rural reporting team, but actually rural New Zealand as well. This is a bit of a kick in the guts for us and someone needs to sort it out. And I guess the broadcasting minister is the first port of call."
As a South Island sheep and beef farmer, Patterson said he'd grown up listening to the public broadcaster.
"Since day dot, it's always been on, the rural news has always been part of that. It's not something we consider them doing nice to have. It's a critical service for us.

"The team do a great job, actually, and certainly not only as a farmer, but as a politician, they've always been fair and reasonable in terms of inquisitive and interested in what's happening in rural New Zealand.
"So we always feel like we get a fair shake - from the rural team anyway. I'd be absolutely devastated to see it going."

The comments from Patterson followed criticism of the RNZ proposal from Federated Farmers, with North Canterbury president Bex Green saying rural New Zealand was already losing its local newspapers and other sources of news, and "now our state broadcaster is looking to abandon us too".
A RNZ spokesperson had responded Thursday, saying: "We will continue to produce news and stories relevant to rural communities."

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/record-br: Two American best friends have set a Guinness World Record by playing a game of chess at the top of a mountain in Ecuador.
Adam Wininger, 32, and Joshua Host, 44, played on the summit of Chimborazo, in the Bolívar region of Ecuador, on 31 March 2026.
The summit is 6,277 metres (20,593 feet) above sea level. That’s more than one and a half times the height of Aoraki Mount Cook, New Zealand’s tallest maunga.
It earned them the record for the highest altitude, or height above sea level, for playing a board game.
The pair first tried to climb the mountain a few months earlier, but bad weather stopped them from reaching the top.
“It’s our favourite game and there is something so epic about playing it on top of a mountain,” Wininger told Guinness World Records.
They beat the old record by about 61 metres (200 feet), which is roughly the height of a 20-storey building.
Britons Tim Maw and Neil Laughton set that record in 2024, when they played at 6,216 metres (20,393 feet) on Putha Hiunchuli in Nepal.
The new record holders say they plan to keep their title. “If someone ever beats us, we’ll beat them by another 200 feet. Every time,” Wininger said.

Kua whakatūria he Guinness World Record e ētahi hoa tata tokorua nō Amerika, i tā rāua tākaro chess ki te tihi o tētahi maunga i Ecuador.
I tākaro a Adam Wininger, 32 ōna tau, rāua ko Joshua Host, 44 ōna tau, ki te tihi o Chimborazo, i te rohe o Bolívar, i Ecuador, i te 31 o Māehe 2026.
E 6,277 mita (20,593 putu) te teitei o te tihi i runga ake i te mata o te moana. He nui ake tēnā i te kotahi me te hāwhe o te teitei o Aoraki, te maunga teitei rawa o Aotearoa.
Nā tēnei i riro ai i a rāua te rekoata mō te tākaro kēmu papa i te wāhi teitei rawa i runga ake i te mata o te moana.
I ngana tuatahi rāua ki te piki i te maunga i ētahi marama i mua, engari nā te kino o te huarere, kāore i taea e rāua te tae ki te tihi.
“Ko tā māua kēmu tino pai tēnei, ā, he mea mīharo rawa te tākaro ki runga i te tihi o te maunga,” te kī a Wininger ki a Guinness World Records.
I hinga i a rāua te rekoata tawhito mā te 61 mita (200 putu) pea, he rite ki te teitei o tētahi whare 20 papa.
Nā ngā tāngata nō Piritana, a Tim Maw rāua ko Neil Laughton, taua rekoata i whakatū i te tau 2024, i tā rāua tākaro i te 6,216 mita (20,393 putu) ki runga o Putha Hiunchuli, i Nepal.
E ai ki ngā kaipupuri hou o te rekoata, ka mau tonu i a rāua tō rāua taitara. “Ki te hinga tō māua rekoata i tētahi, ka hinga anō i a māua tōna mā tētahi atu 200 putu. I ia wā,” te kī a Wininger.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/pakistans: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has become the first person from Pakistan to travel into orbit, and the first astronaut from outside China to visit its Tiangong space station.
The 40-year-old blasted off on a Chinese-made rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, and docked at the space station early on Wednesday.
A space station is like a giant science lab that circles high above Earth, where astronauts live and do experiments.
Ali will stay for five to 10 days, which is much shorter than the six months Chinese astronauts usually spend there. He trained in China for months to get ready, and even learned to speak Chinese.
“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the trip was “the journey of 240 million Pakistanis”. That’s about how many people live in Pakistan.
The mission also matters to China, which wants to show the world that other countries can use Tiangong for research too.

China hopes to land an astronaut on the Moon by 2030. The United States aims to send people back there in 2028, for the first time since 1972. China also plans to build a research base on the Moon with Russia by 2035.
Both China and the United States say they only want to use space peacefully.
Upoko: Kua eke te kaiarorangi tuatahi o Pakistan ki te teihana ātea o Haina
Ko Muhammad Zeeshan Ali te tangata tuatahi nō Pakistan kua haere ki te ātea huri ai i te ao. Ko ia hoki te kaiarorangi tuatahi nō waho o Haina kua toro ki tana teihana ātea, ki Tiangong.

I rere atu te tāne 40 tau te pakeke i runga i tētahi tākirirangi i hangaia e Haina, mai i te Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre i te raki-mā-uru o Haina. I hono atu ia ki te teihana ātea i te atatū o te Wenerei.
He rite te teihana ātea ki tētahi taiwhanga pūtaiao nui e huri haere ana i runga noa atu i te ao. Ka noho ngā kaiarorangi ki reira, ā, ka mahi whakamātau rātou.

Ka noho a Ali ki reira mō te rima ki te 10 rā. He wā poto ake tēnā i ngā marama e ono e noho ai ngā kaiarorangi o Haina i te nuinga o te wā. He maha ngā marama i whakangungu ai ia i Haina kia rite ai ia, ā, i ako hoki ia ki te kōrero i te reo Haina.
“Ehara i te mea mōku anō tēnei rerenga. Kei runga i tōku pokohiwi te ingoa o Pakistan,” te kī a Ali ki ngā kairīpoata i te Tūrei.
I kī te Pirimia o Pakistan, a Shehbaz Sharif, ko tēnei “te haerenga o ngā tāngata 240 miriona o Pakistan”. Koinā tata te maha o ngā tāngata e noho ana ki Pakistan.
He mea nui hoki tēnei mō Haina. E hiahia ana a Haina ki te whakaatu ki te ao ka taea hoki e ētahi atu whenua te whakamahi i Tiangong mō te rangahau.

E hiahia ana a Haina kia tau tētahi o ōna kaiarorangi ki te Marama hei te tau 2030. E whai ana a Amerika kia hoki anō he tāngata ki reira hei te tau 2028, te wā tuatahi mai i te tau 1972. Kei te whakamahere hoki a Haina rāua ko Rūhia ki te hanga i tētahi pokapū rangahau ki te Marama hei te tau 2035.
E kī ana a Haina me Amerika, ko te rangimārie anake te take o ā rāua mahi ki te ātea.

“It’s our favourite game and there is something so epic about playing it on top of a mountain,” Wininger told Guinness World Records.
He joked that if anyone ever beats their record, the pair will simply climb even higher to reclaim it, by exactly 200 feet every time.
For now, the chess-loving duo can enjoy their spot in the record books, all the way up in the clouds.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/spacecraf: A European spacecraft has sent back the first close-up pictures of an asteroid that was deliberately smashed into by a NASA spacecraft, as part of a test to protect Earth one day.
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system this week and released its first detailed images on 25 November 2026.

Dimorphos is a small “moonlet” asteroid that orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos. Back in 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft called DART into Dimorphos, in the first-ever test of what scientists call “planetary defence.”

The idea is simple: if a dangerous asteroid were ever heading towards Earth, could humans crash something into it to change its path and keep our planet safe? The DART test showed that it can work. The impact changed Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos by just over 30 minutes.
Now Hera’s job is to study the crater DART left behind, to help scientists understand exactly what happened and how big the effect was.
“ESA’s Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know,” said mission lead Patrick Michel.
Hera will stay at the asteroid system for months, using cameras and other instruments to learn more about how to keep Earth safe from space rocks in the future.

At Hauraki Intermediate, students use tablets in some lessons and notebooks in others. In science, they research facts quickly and record results in digital tables. In English, however, many still prefer to plan ideas by hand before typing them up. Teachers say technology is useful when it helps students learn more clearly, but it should not replace thinking or discussion. The school has found that the best lessons are those where students use the right tool for the task. In other words, tablets are helpful, but learning works best when they are part of a balanced approach.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-fer: The Black Ferns will take women’s rugby to three New Zealand towns that rarely get to host international test matches, as part of their 2027 home season.

Coach Whitney Hansen’s side will play New Zealand against Canada in Nelson on 10 April, the Black Ferns’ first-ever test in the city. A week later, on 17 April, they’ll face the United States in Timaru, another first for the team.
The third home test will be against Australia in Palmerston North on 21 April, for the O’Reilly Cup. It will be the Black Ferns’ first appearance in the city since 1999.
“We’re excited to take the Black Ferns to communities that don’t often get the chance to host us,” Hansen said.
The regional tests come before a huge year for the Black Ferns, which is also expected to include the first-ever British & Irish Lions Women’s Series.
Hansen said the tour is about helping build momentum for what’s shaping up to be a special year for the team, both on and off the field.
Rugby fans in Nelson, Timaru and Palmerston North will get a rare chance to cheer on New Zealand’s top women’s rugby stars in person, without having to travel to one of the country’s bigger cities.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/christchu: A 25-year-old model and entrepreneur from Christchurch has placed fifth at the 75th Miss Universe pageant, New Zealand’s best result at the competition in more than 40 years.

Georgia Waddington represented New Zealand against contestants from 116 countries and territories at the grand final, held on 25 November 2026. She had been widely tipped by pageant experts as a frontrunner before the final.
For the national costume section of the competition, Waddington wore an outfit inspired by the Pink and White Terraces, a famous natural wonder that was destroyed when Mt Tarawera erupted in 1886.
The crown this year went to Miss Puerto Rico, Jennifer Barreto, with Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela also making the top five.

New Zealand hasn’t placed this well at Miss Universe since 1983, when Lorraine Downes became the only Kiwi to ever win the title. Since then, only a handful of New Zealand representatives have made it into the top rankings.

Before this year, New Zealand hadn’t placed in the competition since 1992, when Lisa Marie de Montalk reached the top 10. That makes Waddington’s fifth-place finish an even bigger milestone for the country.
Waddington’s result is already being celebrated back home as a proud moment for New Zealand on the world stage.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/jordie-ba: All Blacks star Jordie Barrett has been named a finalist for World Rugby’s Player of the Year award, one of rugby’s biggest individual honours.
Barrett is one of four players in the running, along with France’s Louis Bielle-Biarrey and South Africans Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche. Marx is the reigning champion, having won the award last year.
The finalists were announced on Tuesday, ahead of an awards ceremony expected later this month. If Barrett wins, he would be the first All Black to take out the award since Ardie Savea in 2023.

Fellow All Black Peter Lakai has also been nominated, for World Rugby’s Try of the Year award. His try came during New Zealand’s big 50-19 win over Australia at Eden Park in October, when the All Blacks kept hold of the Bledisloe Cup.
In the move, Barrett won a contest for a high ball, before passing to teammate Damian McKenzie, who broke through the Wallabies’ defence and set up Lakai to score.
It caps off a strong year for New Zealand rugby, with two Kiwi players now up for some of the sport’s most prestigious individual prizes.
Fans will have to wait to find out whether Barrett and Lakai can bring the awards home, with winners usually revealed once the busy November international rugby window wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.
